title: Why Can't I Just Be Happy for Them?
theme: Envy, comparison, gratitude, God's grace, trusting God's ways, and the privilege of laboring in His vineyard
opening: Yesterday I heard a story about a group of workers. Some worked all day. Others showed up near the end. And then, incredibly, they were all paid the same amount.  My first reaction? That isn't fair.
prayer: Lord, I give You the parts of my heart that compare, envy, judge, and keep score. When another person receives something beautiful, teach me to see Your goodness rather than my lack. When my first thought is not the person I want to be, help me give it immediately to You and choose another. Replace comparison with gratitude, jealousy with joy, and resentment with generosity. I do not understand all Your ways, nor do I need to. You called me into Your vineyard. Help me remember the privilege of being here, recognize Your grace in the lives of others, and use whatever time remains to labor faithfully for You. Amen.
body:
Yesterday at Mass, as the priest began speaking about the Gospel of the laborers in the vineyard, he pointed out something almost uncomfortable in its honesty. When we first hear this parable, many of us probably understand immediately why the workers who had labored all day were upset.

They worked longer. They endured the heat. Then those who arrived at the end of the day received the same wage.

Something inside us says, That isn't fair.

Maybe it is envy. Maybe jealousy. Maybe comparison. Maybe simply our deeply ingrained understanding that greater effort should receive greater reward.

But then the priest said something that changed the way I heard the parable: How magnificent simply to have been called to work in His vineyard.

That stayed with me.

The workers who arrived early had something the others didn't. They had spent the entire day in the vineyard. Yet instead of seeing that as a privilege, they looked at what someone else received and suddenly felt that what they had been given was not enough.

I recognize that tendency, and frankly, I am sick of it in myself.

Why isn't our first reaction happiness for the other laborer?

Why can't I simply rejoice when someone finds a wonderful job, remodels a beautiful home, receives an unexpected opportunity, or walks into work bright and cheerful despite carrying burdens I know nothing about?

Why does comparison sometimes arrive before gratitude?

I can only speak for myself. Perhaps you don't experience this. But I suspect I am not alone.

And today's other readings seem almost perfectly placed around this uncomfortable part of the Gospel.

Isaiah tells us:

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways.”

As high as the heavens are above the earth, so are God's ways above ours.

Perhaps that is where my questioning has to begin.

I want to understand why I react the way I do. Is it pride? Insecurity? Original sin? Some human instinct toward competition and survival? Is comparison somehow our attempt to reassure ourselves that we are doing well enough?

Maybe pieces of those explanations are true.

But perhaps I don't need to understand every mechanism inside the human heart before asking God to transform mine.

Because the vineyard exposes something much simpler.

I stop looking at the Landowner and start looking at the other laborers.

I begin calculating.

How long did she work? What did he receive? Why does their life look easier? Why did that opportunity come to them? Haven't I worked hard too?

And somewhere in all that accounting, I forget something extraordinary:

I am already standing in God's vineyard.

I was called.

I was invited in.

I have been allowed to labor for Him.

And grace is already all around me.

Then Paul takes this even further in Philippians. His words are astonishing: “For to me life is Christ, and death is gain.” He admits being caught between the two. He longs to depart and be with Christ, yet understands that remaining in the flesh is necessary for the benefit of others.

In other words: there is still work in the vineyard.

That gives our time here an entirely different meaning.

Maybe the question isn't, Why does that laborer have what I don't have?

Maybe it is:

Lord, what would You have me do while I am still in Your vineyard?

That doesn't magically eliminate envy or comparison. I wish it did.

Those thoughts can still appear before I want them to. But perhaps the first thought that enters my mind doesn't have to become the place where I remain.

I can give it to God immediately.

There it is again, Lord. I am comparing. I am jealous. I am wondering why someone else received something I wanted. I don't want this. Take it.

And then perhaps I can deliberately replace it:

Thank You for what You have given them.

Again.

And again.

And again.

Until gratitude becomes stronger than comparison.

Until another person's blessing no longer feels like evidence of my deficiency.

Until I can see God's grace in another person's life without immediately asking what it says about mine.

Perhaps this is part of what it means to labor in the vineyard. We aren't only doing God's work out in the world. God is also doing His work within the laborer.

And maybe that is why I cannot completely dissect the origin of every imperfect reaction within myself.

Isaiah has already reminded me: His thoughts are higher than mine.

I don't have to know everything.

I have to trust the One who does.

And there is tremendous freedom in that.

I don't have to determine what another laborer deserves. I don't have to calculate my position beside theirs. I don't have to understand why God gives one person this and another person that.

I can simply be grateful that when the Landowner came looking for laborers, He called me too.

Whether we arrived early in the morning or in the final hour, what an extraordinary thing it is to find ourselves standing together in His vineyard.

Not competitors.

Not accountants.

Laborers.

And how glorious it is to be one
